items.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: I graduated to Tommy Dorsey... I think I was 17... she went on to sing with Tommy Dorsey... I think you’re talking about — what you’re talking about is the Tommy Dorsey era

ctx.x: What kind of music was played in your house when you were a kid?

Well the first record my father brought home when we got a turntable was “Ain’t Nobody Here But Us Chickens” by Louis Jordan. And I played the death out of that. I loved it. And then later, and my father loved Johann Strauss, he loved German waltzes and stuff like that so he bought some of those records and we heard some of that. And that’s about as heavy as the classical music got in my house at the time. And then we kind of graduated, I kind of graduated to, I graduated to Tommy Dorsey and then to Woody Herman,…
Who you ended up working with. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

items.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: the Charlie Spivak, the Tommy Dorseys and all back in those days before 1962, the musicians always paid for their own hotel.

ctx.x: Well I just said he didn’t seem to make any friends on that particular tour.

Oh I know what it is. So he had told me over the phone. I didn’t have anything written, no nothing written. He told me over the phone he’d pay me $500 a week. And back in those days, back in ’62, that was a good sum of money. So I certainly said yes obviously. I go to get my first paycheck and it’s $400. And the reason it’s $400 is — I don’t know if Benny told me this himself, I can’t remember, or if the secretary, Muriel Zuckerman told me, I’m not sure, but it came from him anyways — he said 500 because he…
